## What Is a Workflow?

A **pipeline** that runs analysis steps for you, in order or in parallel, **without an app running**. Each step runs in its own container on a temporary cloud machine.

**Use it when you need to:** run the same analysis on many files or samples (e.g., genomics), or make it easy to reproduce and share

| Tool | Language | Where you run it |
|---|---|---|
| **Cromwell** | WDL | **Workflows** tab (or an app) |
| **Nextflow** | Nextflow (`.nf`) | **Workflows** tab (or an app) |
| **dsub** | Shell commands, one step | An app's **terminal** |

👉 Most class projects **don't need workflows**: an app is enough. Ready-made workflows: [Dockstore](https://dockstore.org)

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Instructor tip"}
Source: Verily, "Workflows overview" and "Workflow engines". All three tools use the Google Batch API to run tasks, and read and write files in buckets (gs:// paths). Tasks run with the workspace's service account, which can access every bucket in the workspace. Costs (task machines and storage) are billed to the workspace's pod and are not shown in the app cost estimator.
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}

![](<../../Intro to workbench 2.0/images/wf_add.png>){fig-alt="Adding workflow dialog with the workflow source options marked, and the bucket name field and Next button highlighted."}

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
**Step 1: Provide source.** Where's the workflow file?

- **Workspace bucket:** pick **your workspace bucket**. Workbench lists the workflow files it finds there, by folder (search by path).
- **Git repository:** a repo with the workflow (see the [GitHub guide](../extras/github-guide.qmd))

Select the workflow → **Next**

**Step 2: Review details** → add it

Upload the workflow file (`.wdl` or `.nf`) to your bucket **first**. Until there's one to select, **Next** stays grey.
:::
::::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Instructor tip"}
The list may open on the dataproc-staging-aou-rw-… bucket (the staging bucket created for a Spark (Dataproc) app) and say "0 workflows found": choose your workspace bucket (rw-…) in the same list. It then finds .wdl files in all its folders, grouped by folder; search by the start of the path, e.g. data/workflows/. Nextflow workflows should include a nextflow.config file next to the .nf file.
:::

## Running a Workflow

**Setup** tab → select the workflow → **+ New job**

1. **Job details:** a name, and *Run a single job* (or a batch)
2. **Inputs:** a **form**, one box per input in the workflow. `gs://` paths for files; plain text (no quotation marks) for strings
3. **Outputs:** your bucket, and a folder named after the job
4. **Submit job**, then follow it on **Job status**: *Starting* → *Running* → *Completed*

**Batch jobs:** run one WDL workflow **many times in parallel**, e.g., once per sample

- Choose *Run a batch job with inputs defined by an input table*
- Upload a **CSV** (one row per run), then match its columns to the workflow's inputs

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Instructor tip"}
Source: Verily, "Use the Cromwell engine to run WDL workflows" and "Create batch jobs". Cromwell call caching is on by default, so re-running reuses results from steps that already finished; deleting intermediate files is also on by default; keep both. Results go to <bucket>/<job name>/<workflow>/<job ID>/call-<task>/. Limits: 1,000 outstanding jobs per user and 5,000 submitted in 24 hours; for a batch, the limit applies to each job, and a batch that exceeds it is rejected entirely. Genomic Variant Store (GVS) is an example of a large WDL workflow from the Broad Institute; Verily has a guide for it.
:::

## dsub: Jobs from an App

For **one-step** jobs, e.g., run a command on many files. dsub is ready to use in *All of Us* Jupyter apps. In *All of Us*, every job needs the **network** settings, **no public address**, and an image from the ***All of Us* mirror**:

```{.bash code-line-numbers="false"}
export DSUB_CLOUD_SDK_IMAGE=gcr.io/google.com/cloudsdktool/google-cloud-cli:591.0.0-slim
MIRROR=us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/all-of-us-rw-prod/aou-rw-gar-remote-repo-docker-prod

dsub --provider google-batch \
  --project "${GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT}" --user-project "${GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT}" \
  --regions us-central1 --use-private-address \
  --network global/networks/network \
  --subnetwork regions/us-central1/subnetworks/subnetwork \
  --service-account "$(gcloud config get-value account)" \
  --logging gs://<your-bucket>/logs/ \
  --input  BAM=gs://<your-bucket>/sample.bam \
  --output BAI=gs://<your-bucket>/sample.bam.bai \
  --image  "${MIRROR}/biocontainers/samtools:<version>" \
  --command 'samtools index ${BAM} ${BAI}' \
  --wait
```

👉 A full class, tested in *All of Us*: [Running Workflows](../extras/workflows-dsub.qmd). More examples: tutorial notebook `05_How_to_use_workflow_tools` (dsub, Cromwell, Nextflow)

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Instructor tip"}
Source: Verily, "Run dsub jobs", and the All of Us tutorial notebooks. Tested November 2026 in an All of Us Jupyter app (dsub 0.5.6, CDR v9). Without --use-private-address and the network settings, jobs can't start inside the perimeter; with it, images must come from Google registries, so Docker Hub images go through the All of Us mirror. DSUB_CLOUD_SDK_IMAGE pins dsub's helper image: Cloud SDK version 592 (3 November 2026) made every job fail with exit status 127. PET_SA_EMAIL was empty in our app; gcloud config get-value account gives the account to use. Each dsub job starts its own cloud machine, billed to your pod.
:::
